title: Grade 12 Chemistry — Surface Chemistry
description: Adsorption, colloids, emulsions, gels, and catalysis types
subject: chemistry

questions.question: Adsorption is the process where:
options: A substance is absorbed into the bulk of another
A substance accumulates on the surface of another (solid or liquid)
Two substances react chemically at a surface
A gas dissolves in a liquid
questions.explanation: Adsorption: accumulation of substance on a surface. Absorptate = substance adsorbed; adsorbent = surface. Absorption: substance goes into the BULK. Adsorption is a surface phenomenon.

questions.question: Physisorption (physical adsorption) differs from chemisorption in that physisorption:
options: Involves weak van der Waals forces, is reversible, and occurs at low temperatures
questions.explanation: Physisorption: weak van der Waals forces, reversible, low ΔH (20–40 kJ/mol), occurs at low T, multilayer possible. Chemisorption: strong chemical bonds, irreversible, high ΔH (40–400 kJ/mol), occurs at high T, monolayer.

questions.question: Freundlich adsorption isotherm is: x/m = ?
questions.explanation: Freundlich isotherm: x/m = kP^(1/n). x = mass adsorbed, m = mass of adsorbent, P = pressure. At low P: linear. At high P: x/m approaches constant. Empirical equation (not theoretically derived).

questions.question: A colloid is a dispersion where the particle size is approximately:
questions.explanation: Colloidal particles: 1–1000 nm (1–1000 × 10⁻⁹ m). True solutions < 1 nm (ions/molecules). Suspensions > 1000 nm (particles visible, settle). Colloids don't settle due to Brownian motion.

questions.question: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by:
options: Colloidal particles (large enough to scatter visible light)
questions.explanation: Tyndall effect: colloidal particles scatter light, making the beam visible. True solutions don't show it (particles too small). Used to distinguish colloid from true solution. Example: beam of light in foggy air.

questions.question: Brownian motion in colloids is caused by:
options: Random bombardment of colloidal particles by solvent molecules — keeps them in suspension
questions.explanation: Brownian motion: random zigzag movement of colloidal particles due to unequal bombardment by solvent molecules. It prevents settling (sedimentation). First observed by Robert Brown (1827) with pollen grains.

questions.question: Coagulation (precipitation) of a colloid is caused by:
options: Adding electrolytes — oppositely charged ions neutralise colloidal charge, causing aggregation
questions.explanation: Colloidal particles are stabilised by similar charges (repel each other). Adding an electrolyte provides oppositely charged ions → neutralises charge → particles attract → coagulate. Hardy-Schulze rule: higher valence ion = more effective coagulation.

questions.question: An emulsion is a colloid of:
questions.explanation: Emulsion: liquid dispersed in liquid. Oil-in-water (O/W): e.g., milk, mayonnaise, cream. Water-in-oil (W/O): e.g., butter, cold cream. Emulsifying agents (soaps) stabilise emulsions.

questions.question: Homogeneous catalysis means:
options: Catalyst and reactants are in different phases
Catalyst and reactants are in the SAME phase
The rate increases only at high temperature
questions.explanation: Homogeneous catalysis: catalyst and reactants in same phase. Example: H₂SO₄ (aq) catalysing ester hydrolysis in solution; NO(g) catalysing SO₂ oxidation in gas phase. Heterogeneous: different phases (Ni solid + gas reactants).

questions.question: Enzyme catalysis is an example of:
options: Biological/enzymatic catalysis — extremely specific, efficient at body temperature
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts (proteins). Features: high specificity (one enzyme, one substrate — lock-and-key), very efficient, mild conditions (37°C, neutral pH). Example: amylase digests starch.

questions.question: Peptization is the process of:
options: Converting a fresh precipitate back into a colloid by adding a small amount of electrolyte
Making a colloid from a solution
questions.explanation: Peptization: a precipitate is converted into a colloid (sol) by adding a small amount of electrolyte (the peptizing agent). The electrolyte ions are preferentially adsorbed, giving particles similar charges that repel.

questions.question: The charge on As₂S₃ sol (prepared in excess H₂S) is:
questions.explanation: As₂S₃ sol prepared in H₂S: excess S²⁻ ions are adsorbed → negatively charged particles. Contrast: Fe(OH)₃ sol in FeCl₃ adsorbs Fe³⁺ → positively charged. Charge determines coagulation behaviour.

questions.question: Lyophilic colloids ('solvent-loving') are characterised by:
options: Strong interaction with solvent — stable, reversible (can be reconstituted after drying)
questions.explanation: Lyophilic: strong affinity for solvent (hydrophilic in water). Stable, not easily coagulated. Examples: starch, gelatin, gum arabic. Lyophobic: weak affinity, easily coagulated (gold sol, Fe(OH)₃ sol).

questions.question: Langmuir adsorption isotherm assumes:
options: Monolayer adsorption on uniform surface — fixed number of identical adsorption sites
questions.explanation: Langmuir isotherm: monolayer adsorption on uniform surface with identical sites; no interactions between adsorbed molecules; fixed number of sites. θ = bP/(1+bP) where θ = fraction of sites occupied.

questions.question: The cleansing action of soap is due to:
options: Its amphiphilic structure — hydrophobic tail dissolves in oil; hydrophilic head stays in water forming micelles
questions.explanation: Soap (sodium/potassium fatty acid salt): hydrophobic tail (fatty acid chain) dissolves in oil/grease; hydrophilic head (−COO⁻Na⁺) stays in water. Oil droplets surrounded by soap molecules (micelles) → emulsified and washed away.
